title: Lord of the Sabbath, Greater Than Jonah
summary: Two Sabbath disputes, over picking grain and healing a withered hand, lead the Pharisees to plot Jesus' death. Matthew presents Jesus as Isaiah's gentle Servant. When the Pharisees say he drives out demons by Beelzebul, Jesus answers that he binds the strong man by the Spirit of God, warns against blasphemy against the Spirit, refuses them any sign but Jonah's, and declares that those who do the Father's will are his true family.
story:
Chapter 11 ended with Jesus' invitation to find rest under his easy yoke. Chapter 12 opens ‘at that time’ (the same phrase as 11:25) with a fight about the day of rest itself. The rejection that chapter 11 described now hardens into open conflict, and for the first time Matthew says the Pharisees plotted how to kill Jesus (verse 14). The charge that Jesus drives out demons by the prince of demons, first voiced in 9:34, is now answered at length. By the end of the chapter lines are drawn: those who oppose him, a generation that demands signs, and a new family made up of those who do the Father's will.

The chapter belongs to the section that runs from 11:2 to 13:53, in which Jesus' reception is the question. Its conflicts set up the parables of chapter 13, which begin on the same day (13:1) and explain why the word of the kingdom is received by some and refused by others. Several threads look ahead: the plot of verse 14 is the first step toward the passion, the sign of Jonah points to the resurrection, and the Servant who proclaims justice to the nations anticipates the mission to all nations in 28:19.
historical:
The Sabbath, the seventh day, was a sign of the covenant between God and Israel (Exodus 31:13-17), and in the centuries before Jesus it had become a mark of Jewish identity under pressure. In the Maccabean revolt of the 160s BC a group of the faithful let themselves be killed rather than defend themselves on the Sabbath, after which Mattathias and his followers decided to fight if attacked (1 Maccabees 2:29-41). Teachers therefore worked to define forbidden work. The Mishnah, compiled around AD 200 from earlier debates, lists thirty-nine main categories of work, among them reaping, threshing, and winnowing (m. Shabbat 7:2); plucking heads of grain and rubbing them in the hands (Luke 6:1) could be classed as reaping and threshing. The Law allowed a hungry passer-by to pluck grain by hand from a neighbor's field (Deuteronomy 23:25), so the Pharisees' objection concerns the day, not theft.

Jewish teachers agreed that danger to life overrides the Sabbath (m. Yoma 8:6), and they debated how far to go in lesser cases. The Damascus Document from Qumran forbids lifting an animal out of a pit on the Sabbath (CD 11:13-14), while a later rabbinic ruling allows bringing cushions and bedding so that an animal fallen into a ditch can climb out itself (b. Shabbat 128b). Jesus' question in verse 11 assumes his hearers would rescue the sheep. A withered hand was not an emergency and could have waited until evening, which is why the healing was a test case. A saying attributed to Rabbi Simeon ben Menasya, that the Sabbath is given to you and you are not given to the Sabbath (Mekhilta on Exodus 31:13), closely resembles Mark 2:27, which Matthew does not include.

Jesus' answers appeal to Scripture. David, fleeing from Saul, received the bread of the Presence from the priest Ahimelech at Nob (1 Samuel 21:1-6); Mark 2:26 names Abiathar, and Matthew and Luke leave the priest unnamed. The priests worked every Sabbath, offering the additional Sabbath sacrifices (Numbers 28:9-10) and replacing the bread of the Presence (Leviticus 24:8), and no one accused them of breaking the day. Hosea 6:6, ‘I desire mercy, not sacrifice’, is quoted only by Matthew among the evangelists, here and in 9:13. After the temple fell in AD 70, the rabbinic tradition remembered Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai consoling his disciple Joshua among the ruins with the same verse: acts of loving-kindness atone as sacrifices once did (Avot de-Rabbi Natan A 4).

Exorcism was practiced by other Jews, which gives force to verse 27. Tobit 8:2-3 tells of a demon driven off by the smoke of a fish's heart and liver, and Josephus describes a Jew named Eleazar drawing a demon out of a man before Vespasian with a ring and a root prescribed by Solomon (Antiquities 8.45-49). The Queen of the South is the queen of Sheba (1 Kings 10:1-13), usually located in Saba in southwest Arabia; Josephus calls her queen of Egypt and Ethiopia (Antiquities 8.165), and Ethiopian tradition later claimed her. Nineveh, the Assyrian capital, destroyed in 612 BC, was remembered as Israel's enemy that repented at Jonah's preaching (Jonah 3). The parallels are Mark 2:23-3:12 and 3:20-35, and Luke 6:1-11, 8:19-21, 11:14-32, and 12:10.
cultural:
The bread of the Presence was twelve loaves set out every Sabbath on a table in the holy place and eaten afterward by the priests alone (Leviticus 24:5-9). Temple and Sabbath were Israel's two great holy institutions, one sacred space and the other sacred time, and in verses 5 to 8 Jesus claims authority over both.

Beelzebul was a name for the ruler of demons. It is related to Baal-zebub, ‘lord of flies’, the god of Ekron consulted by King Ahaziah (2 Kings 1:2), which many scholars take as Israel's mocking alteration of Baal-zebul, ‘Prince Baal’, a title known from Ugaritic texts; zebul can also mean an exalted house (1 Kings 8:13), which suits Jesus' reply about a divided house and a strong man's house. To say that someone's power came from the prince of demons was to accuse him of sorcery, a capital crime in the law (Exodus 22:18, Deuteronomy 18:10-12). The charge outlived Jesus: Justin Martyr reports that opponents called him a magician (Dialogue with Trypho 69), and a tradition in the Babylonian Talmud remembers him as executed for sorcery and leading Israel astray (Sanhedrin 43a). No ancient opponent denied that he did remarkable things; the dispute was over their source.

The strong man's house draws on Isaiah 49:24-25, where the Lord asks whether plunder can be snatched from the mighty and answers that he himself will take the captives of the mighty. Waterless places were thought to be haunts of demons and desert creatures (Isaiah 13:21, 34:14), and in Tobit 8:3 the demon Asmodeus flees to the remotest parts of Egypt. A house ‘swept clean, and put in order’ but empty was an invitation to a worse occupant. ‘Brood of vipers’ repeats John the Baptist's words (3:7). The ‘careless word’ (argos, idle, useless) of verse 36 is speech that does nothing, and the day of judgment weighs it because words reveal the heart.

Jewish time was counted inclusively, so that any part of a day could count as the whole. Rabbi Eleazar ben Azariah, around AD 100, is remembered as saying that a day and a night make an onah, a period of time, and that part of an onah counts as the whole (y. Shabbat 9:3, b. Pesahim 4a). In Esther 4:16 and 5:1 a fast of three days, night or day, ends on the third day, and in 1 Samuel 30:12-13 ‘three days and three nights’ is the same as ‘three days ago’.

Family loyalty was among the strongest bonds in the ancient Mediterranean world, bound up with honor, inheritance, work, and care in old age. Relatives who stood outside and sent for a teacher expected him to come out, and a son who put his circle of disciples ahead of his mother and brothers would have seemed to shame them. A teacher's disciples sat around him to learn, and the Mishnah counsels sitting in the dust at the feet of the sages (m. Avot 1:4).
literary:
The chapter alternates conflict and interpretation. Two Sabbath controversies (verses 1 to 14) end in a death plot. Matthew then halts the action for the longest of his formula quotations, Isaiah 42:1-4 (verses 18 to 21), which explains Jesus' withdrawal and his command to silence and shows what kind of Messiah he is. The Beelzebul controversy (verses 22 to 37) and the demand for a sign (verses 38 to 45) bring the conflict to a head, and the scene with Jesus' family (verses 46 to 50) turns the chapter's question from who opposes him to who belongs to him.

Matthew has shaped Mark's material. To the grainfield dispute he adds the priests in the temple, the saying about something greater than the temple, and Hosea 6:6 (verses 5 to 7); to the healing he adds the sheep in the pit (verses 11 and 12). He omits Mark's note that Jesus' family thought he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21). The demand for a sign here is repeated in shorter form in 16:1-4. The phrase ‘greater’ runs through the chapter: something greater than the temple (verse 6), than Jonah (verse 41), and than Solomon (verse 42), so that Jesus surpasses the priesthood's sanctuary, the prophet, and the wise king. Houses also recur: the house of God (verse 4), the divided household (verse 25), the strong man's house (verse 29), and the empty house (verse 44), and the chapter ends with Jesus defining his own household.

Matthew's form of Isaiah 42:1-4 matches neither the Hebrew nor the Greek Old Testament exactly. The Septuagint names the servant as Jacob and the chosen as Israel; Matthew has neither. Where the Hebrew says ‘whom I uphold, My Chosen One’, Matthew has ‘whom I have chosen, My beloved, in whom My soul delights’, echoing the voice at Jesus' baptism (3:17) and anticipating the transfiguration (17:5). He renders the servant's quietness with ‘He will not quarrel’, omits the first half of Isaiah 42:4, and ends with the Septuagint's ‘in His name the nations will put their hope’ where the Hebrew has ‘in His law the islands will put their hope’. Krister Stendahl (The School of St. Matthew, 1954) argued that such quotations show careful scholarly work on several text forms, and Richard Beaton (Isaiah's Christ in Matthew's Gospel, 2002) argued that the quotation's emphasis on justice shapes Matthew's whole portrait of Jesus.

outline.t: Grain picked on the Sabbath: Lord of the Sabbath
A withered hand healed; the plot to kill Jesus
The Beelzebul accusation and the strong man bound
Blasphemy against the Spirit; words and the heart
The sign of Jonah and the returning spirit

doctrines.note: Jesus does not abolish the Sabbath but interprets it by God's purpose: mercy, rest, and doing good (verse 12). As Lord of the Sabbath he claims authority over the day's meaning, and he reads it through Hosea 6:6. Christians differ on how the Sabbath command binds the church, whether as a principle fulfilled in Christ's rest, as a moral law transferred to the Lord's Day, or as the seventh day still to be kept, but all read it in the light of this chapter's mercy.

The crowds ask whether Jesus is the Son of David (verse 23), and Matthew answers with Isaiah's Servant, chosen, beloved, and anointed with the Spirit, who brings justice to the nations without quarreling or crushing the weak. The Messiah is greater than temple, prophet, and king, yet his way is gentleness.

Jesus drives out demons by the Spirit of God, and that is the sign that God's kingdom has arrived (verse 28), fulfilling the promise that God would put his Spirit on his Servant (verse 18). To call the Spirit's plain work demonic, and to persist in that verdict, is to refuse the very means by which God forgives (verses 31 and 32).

The kingdom comes as an invasion: Jesus enters the strong man's house, binds him, and plunders his goods (verse 29). Satan's hold on people is being broken now, which leaves no neutral ground: “He who is not with Me is against Me” (verse 30). The kingdom has ‘come upon you’ (phthanō) in Jesus' works, though its fullness is still to come.

Jesus defines his family as those who do the will of his Father in heaven (verse 50). This does not reject his natural family, who appear among the believers in Acts 1:14, but establishes a new household of disciples in which men and women alike are brother, sister, and mother to him, and so to one another.

words.note: Sabbaton, Sabbath, from the Hebrew shabbat, related to the verb shavat, to cease or rest. It occurs about sixty-eight times in the New Testament, eleven in Matthew, eight of them in this chapter. The plural can mean the Sabbath day or a week. The day recalled God's rest after creation (Exodus 20:11) and Israel's release from slavery (Deuteronomy 5:15). Jesus' disputes are not about whether to keep it but about what keeping it means.

Eleos, mercy, compassion shown in action. It occurs about twenty-seven times in the New Testament, three in Matthew (9:13, 12:7, 23:23). In Hosea 6:6 it renders the Hebrew hesed, the covenant love and loyal kindness God shows and asks of his people. Jesus accuses his critics of not knowing what the verse means: God's commands exist for mercy, and a reading of the law that condemns the hungry and the sick has missed their purpose. In 23:23 mercy is one of ‘the weightier matters of the law’.

Pais, child, boy, or servant. It occurs about twenty-four times in the New Testament, eight in Matthew. In verse 18 it renders Isaiah's ‘servant of the LORD’, and the Septuagint uses pais throughout Isaiah's Servant passages. The same word was used for the centurion's servant (8:6) and for the boys in the temple (21:15). Because pais can mean both child and servant, early Christians could call Jesus God's ‘holy servant’ (Acts 3:13, 4:27) in a way that suggested sonship as well.

Phthanō, to arrive, to come before, to reach. It occurs seven times in the New Testament. In verse 28 the aorist ephthasen says that the kingdom of God ‘has come upon you’, has already reached you, in Jesus' exorcisms. It is one of the clearest sayings about the kingdom as present, set beside sayings that it is ‘near’ (4:17) and still to come (6:10). ‘Kingdom of God’ is rare in Matthew, who usually says ‘kingdom of heaven’, and its use here may stress that God himself is at work.

Ischuros, strong, mighty, powerful. It occurs about twenty-nine times in the New Testament. In verse 29 the ‘strong man’ is Satan, who holds people captive, and the one who binds him must be stronger. John the Baptist had announced a coming one ‘more powerful’ than himself, using the comparative of this word (3:11), and Luke's parallel says a stronger one attacks and overpowers him (Luke 11:22). Isaiah 49:24-25 lies behind the image of taking plunder from the mighty.

Blasphēmia, slander, abusive speech, blasphemy. It occurs about eighteen times in the New Testament, four in Matthew (twice in verse 31, and 15:19 and 26:65). Against people it means slander; against God it means speaking of him falsely or with contempt. At Jesus' trial the high priest will charge Jesus himself with blasphemy (26:65). In verses 31 and 32 it names the Pharisees' act of attributing the Spirit's work to Satan.

Sēmeion, sign, a token that points beyond itself. It occurs about seventy-seven times in the New Testament, thirteen in Matthew. The Pharisees and scribes want a sign on demand, a public proof, after Jesus has already healed the blind and mute. He refuses, offering only ‘the sign of the prophet Jonah’, which Matthew explains as his burial and rising. In John's Gospel the same word is the name for Jesus' miracles, and throughout the New Testament signs confirm faith rather than compel it.

Kētos, a sea monster or huge fish. It occurs only here in the New Testament, in a verbatim quotation of the Septuagint of Jonah (Jonah 2:1 in the Greek and Hebrew numbering, 1:17 in English Bibles), where the Hebrew has dag gadol, a great fish. The King James Version's ‘whale’ comes from older English usage; the Greek names no species. In Greek literature kētos is the monster of the deep, and Jonah's descent into it became an image of descent into death.

christ:
The chapter piles up claims about Jesus that go beyond any prophet's. Something greater than the temple, where God dwelt, is here (verse 6); the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath, which God instituted (verse 8); he is the stronger one who binds Satan (verse 29), greater than Jonah the prophet and Solomon the wise king, son of David (verses 41 and 42). The crowds rightly wonder whether he is the Son of David (verse 23), the title the blind and the Canaanite woman have used in crying for mercy (9:27, 15:22). He knows his opponents' thoughts (verse 25), and he makes loyalty to himself the dividing line of the world: whoever is not with him is against him (verse 30).

Yet the Servant's way is quiet. Matthew quotes Isaiah 42:1-4 at the moment Jesus withdraws from a death plot and tells those he heals not to make him known. The one on whom God has put his Spirit, whom God calls ‘My beloved’ as at the baptism, will not quarrel or cry out, will not break a bruised reed or snuff out a smoldering wick, and in his name the nations will put their hope. Ancient Jewish readers also read Isaiah 42:1 messianically: the Aramaic Targum of Isaiah begins the verse ‘Behold my servant, the Messiah’.

The sign of Jonah is the clearest prediction of Jesus' resurrection so far in Matthew. As Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish and came out alive to preach to Nineveh, so the Son of Man will be ‘in the heart of the earth’ and will rise; that event, not a sign produced on demand, will be God's answer to his accusers. Finally, the one who is Son of the Father in heaven (verse 50) shares his family with all who do the Father's will, so that his disciples become his brothers, sisters, and mother, as the risen Jesus will call them ‘My brothers’ (28:10).
interpretation:
The Sabbath disputes shaped Christian practice early. Ignatius of Antioch, around 110, described believers who no longer kept the Sabbath but lived by the Lord's Day, the day of the resurrection (To the Magnesians 9.1). Calvin taught that the ceremonial side of the Sabbath was fulfilled in Christ while its rest, worship, and relief for workers remained (Institutes 2.8.28-34), and the Westminster Confession (21.8) allowed works of necessity and mercy on the Christian Sabbath in words drawn from this chapter. Abraham Joshua Heschel's The Sabbath (1951) gave modern readers, Jewish and Christian, a picture of the day as a sanctuary in time, which helps explain why the disputes mattered so much.

The Servant quotation has had its own readers. The Targum of Isaiah reads Isaiah 42:1 as ‘my servant, the Messiah’. The Puritan Richard Sibbes built The Bruised Reed (1630) on Isaiah 42:3 and Matthew 12:20, a book of comfort for weak and troubled believers still widely read.

The strong man and the unforgivable sin drew early comment. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.8.2) read the strong man as the devil and Christ as the one who bound him, and Augustine (City of God 20.7) used the saying to interpret the binding of Satan in Revelation 20. Augustine's Sermon 71 identified the sin against the Spirit as final impenitence, and Thomas Aquinas gathered the readings of the Fathers (Summa Theologiae II-II, question 14). Gregory the Great (Dialogues, book 4) reasoned from ‘either in this age or in the one to come’ that some sins can be forgiven after death, one of the texts later cited for purgatory; the Reformers denied that the phrase implies any such forgiveness, reading it as a Semitic way of saying ‘never’. Calvin (Institutes 3.3.22) defined the sin as deliberate resistance to truth known to be God's. John Bunyan's Grace Abounding (1666) records his long terror that he had committed it, and Bertrand Russell's Why I Am Not a Christian (1927) cited the saying as a source of needless misery.

The sign of Jonah was a favorite of early Christian art: Jonah cast out, swallowed, and resting under his vine is among the scenes most often painted in the Roman catacombs and carved on third-century sarcophagi as a picture of resurrection. When pagans mocked the story, Augustine answered in a letter to Deogratias (Letter 102, around 409) that the one who questions this miracle must question them all, and read Jonah's passage from ship to fish as Christ's from cross to tomb. The family scene fed the later debate over Jesus' brothers, and Tertullian (On the Flesh of Christ 7) argued against those who used ‘Who is My mother?’ to deny that Christ was truly born. The Revised Common Lectionary passes from 11:30 to 13:1 in Year A and reads the Beelzebul and family material from Mark 3 in Year B, so much of this chapter is seldom heard on Sundays.
text:
English Bibles differ at several points. In verse 6 the earliest manuscripts read the neuter meizon, ‘something greater than the temple’, while later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read the masculine, ‘one greater’; the neuter may point to the kingdom or the presence of God at work in Jesus, the masculine to Jesus himself. In verse 15 Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus read that ‘many’ followed him, while most manuscripts read ‘large crowds’. In verse 24 the King James Version's Beelzebub follows the Latin and Syriac, which assimilated the name to 2 Kings 1:2; the Greek manuscripts read Beelzeboul or Beezeboul.

Verse 47 is missing from Codex Sinaiticus (in its first hand), Codex Vaticanus, Codex Regius (L), and some early translations. Most editors think it was lost by accident, since both verse 46 and verse 47 end with the same Greek word, lalēsai (‘to speak’), and a copyist's eye could skip from one to the other; the Nestle-Aland edition prints it in brackets, and some modern versions put it in a footnote. In verse 40 the King James Version's ‘whale’ renders kētos, a sea monster, and the quotation of Jonah is Jonah 1:17 in English Bibles but 2:1 in the Hebrew and Greek, which begin chapter 2 one verse earlier. In verse 7 Matthew's eleos, ‘mercy’, agrees with the Septuagint of Hosea 6:6, where the Hebrew is hesed; English versions of Hosea vary between ‘mercy’, ‘steadfast love’, and ‘loving devotion’, which is why the saying can look different in Hosea and in Matthew.

teach.big: Jesus, the gentle Servant who is Lord of the Sabbath and stronger than Satan, divides every hearer into those who reject God's plain work in him and those who do the Father's will and so become his family.

outline.t: God's commands serve mercy; the one greater than the temple interprets the Sabbath, and hunger is not a crime.
Doing good is always lawful, and religion that protects rules while plotting harm has lost its way.
The Messiah's power is gentle: he does not crush the bruised or quench the faint, and his justice reaches the nations.
Jesus' works are the Spirit's invasion of Satan's house, and before him no one stays neutral.
Every sin can be forgiven, except the settled refusal that calls God's saving work evil and so shuts out forgiveness.
Words reveal the heart, and God will weigh even careless ones.
God gives no signs to those who demand them, but he gives the resurrection, and pagans who repented will judge the unrepentant.
A life swept clean but left empty is not safe; reform without the presence of God invites worse.
Those who do the Father's will are Jesus' own family, brother, sister, and mother.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings are common. The first presents the Pharisees as legalists who cared nothing for mercy, and Judaism as a religion of rules; the Pharisees were serious, respected teachers, their debates about Sabbath rescue show real concern for life, and Jesus argues with them from within Israel's Scriptures, as Jewish teachers argued with one another. The second uses the chapter to dismiss rest, worship, and holy time altogether; Jesus claims the Sabbath's meaning, he does not abolish the gift of rest. The third reads verse 30 as a license to treat everyone who disagrees with one's own group as an enemy; the line runs around Jesus, not around a church's preferences, and Mark 9:40 (‘whoever is not against us is for us’) guards the other side.

The warning about blasphemy against the Spirit is the passage most likely to be misused. Preachers should never use it to frighten hearers or suggest that a careless word, a doubt, a blasphemous thought that intrudes unbidden, or a sin before conversion could be unforgivable. The sin in context is the settled verdict of people who saw God's liberating work and called it Satan's. Finally, avoid turning the sign of Jonah into a debate about marine biology or the exact hour of the crucifixion; the point is the Son of Man's death and resurrection and the call to repent at a greater preaching than Jonah's.
teach.pastoral:
This chapter will reach people who fear they have committed the unforgivable sin. Many are believers with sensitive consciences, and some live with scrupulosity, a form of obsessive-compulsive disorder in which intrusive blasphemous thoughts or fears of damnation recur against the person's will and cause great distress. Tell them plainly what pastors from John Bunyan's day to ours have observed: the fear of having committed this sin, and the desire to be right with God, are themselves signs that one has not, since the sin Jesus describes is marked by hardness and contempt, not by anxiety. Remind them that the same passage begins with the widest promise of forgiveness in the Gospels, that every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven. Encourage those whose fears are persistent and tormenting to seek help from a pastor and from a counselor or doctor who understands obsessive-compulsive disorder, since it is treatable and seeking treatment is consistent with trusting God. If the fear has become despair or thoughts of self-harm, they should contact emergency or crisis services at once (in the United States, call or text 988).

The family scene will reach people whose families do not understand or accept their faith, and people who have no family at all. Teach that the church is meant to be the family Jesus describes, and that belonging to it is open to all who do the Father's will. The healing of the withered hand will reach people with disabilities; Jesus restores the man's hand without treating him as a problem to be solved or an object lesson, and the church should treat people with disabilities as members of the family, not as test cases.

hard.q: What is the blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, and can someone commit it without knowing?
hard.a:
The objection is moral as well as exegetical. If God's mercy is boundless and the cross atones for all sin, how can any sin be beyond forgiveness, and why would Jesus speak words that have caused so much fear? Bertrand Russell, in his 1927 lecture Why I Am Not a Christian, singled out this saying as a cause of untold misery to sensitive people who imagined they had committed the sin, and judged that a truly kind teacher would not have spoken it. John Bunyan's Grace Abounding (1666) shows the misery from the inside: for years he believed he had sold Christ and was beyond hope. Some ask further why speaking against the Son of Man can be forgiven while speaking against the Spirit cannot, when Jesus is himself divine.

Christian interpreters answer from the context and from the logic of forgiveness. The Pharisees had watched a blind and mute man freed by the Spirit of God (verses 22 and 28) and declared it the work of Beelzebul. The sin is not a careless word, a doubt, or an intrusive thought, but a settled verdict that calls God's evident work of liberation evil. Augustine (Sermon 71) identified it with final impenitence, the hardness that refuses forgiveness to the end. Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae II-II, question 14) gathered this reading with others, including sin committed out of deliberate malice against the Spirit's grace. Calvin (Institutes 3.3.22) described it as knowing resistance to truth one recognizes to be God's. On all these readings the sin is unforgivable not because God's mercy runs out, but because the person has rejected the very one through whom forgiveness comes and so shut the door. As for the Son of Man, many interpreters suggest that his identity was still veiled in his lowliness and could be misunderstood, as Paul says he himself acted ‘in ignorance’ as a persecutor (1 Timothy 1:13), whereas the Spirit's work in freeing the possessed was plain.

Traditions differ on details: some hold that the sin in its strict form could be committed only by those who saw Jesus' works, others relate it to the warnings of Hebrews 6:4-6 and 10:26-29 and the ‘sin that leads to death’ of 1 John 5:16, and interpreters disagree on how closely those passages connect. All agree on the pastoral point. The passage opens with the promise that every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven, and those who fear they have committed the unforgivable sin show by their fear and their longing for God that they have not.

hard.q: How could Jesus be “three days and three nights in the heart of the earth” if he died on Friday and rose on Sunday morning?
hard.a:
The objection is old and simple. The Gospels place Jesus' death on the day before the Sabbath (Mark 15:42) and the empty tomb early on the first day of the week, which gives, by modern reckoning, about a day and a half: Friday afternoon, Saturday, and part of Sunday. Thomas Paine, in The Age of Reason, part 2 (1795), pressed the point: by the Gospels' own account Jesus was in the grave only one day and two nights, about thirty-six hours instead of seventy-two, so the prediction failed. Skeptics since have listed verse 40 among the Bible's contradictions.

The main response appeals to the way days were counted. Jewish reckoning was inclusive, and any part of a day could stand for the whole. Rabbi Eleazar ben Azariah, around AD 100, is remembered as teaching that a day and a night make one period and that part of such a period counts as the whole (y. Shabbat 9:3, b. Pesahim 4a). Scripture itself uses the idiom loosely: Esther's fast of ‘three days, night or day’ ends ‘on the third day’ (Esther 4:16, 5:1), and an Egyptian who had gone ‘three days and three nights’ without food says he fell ill ‘three days ago’ (1 Samuel 30:12-13). Matthew, who wrote verse 40, also records Jesus' predictions that he would be raised ‘on the third day’ (16:21, 17:23, 20:19) and has his enemies ask for the tomb to be secured ‘until the third day’ because he had said ‘after three days’ (27:63-64), which shows that for Matthew and his readers the phrases meant the same span. Jesus' wording comes straight from Jonah 1:17 and keeps the prophet's phrase for the sake of the comparison. Hosea 6:2, ‘on the third day He will raise us up’, may also stand in the background.

A minority proposes other chronologies. R. A. Torrey (Difficulties in the Bible, 1907) and others argued that Jesus died on Wednesday, taking the Sabbath of John 19:31 as a Passover festival Sabbath, so that a literal seventy-two hours passed before a Saturday evening resurrection; some others propose a Thursday crucifixion. Most historians and commentators, Christian and not, hold the Friday date, which fits the Gospels' ‘day of preparation’ and the early church's observance, and regard the inclusive reading as sufficient. This is a question of chronology, on which Christians may differ, not a question of the resurrection itself, which all four Gospels and Paul (1 Corinthians 15:4) confess.

observe: What two Old Testament examples does Jesus give in verses 3 to 5 to answer the charge about the grainfield, and what does he claim in verses 6 and 8?
How does Matthew's quotation of Isaiah in verses 18 to 21 describe the Servant's manner and mission?
Whom does Jesus call his mother and brothers in verses 49 and 50, and on what basis?
interpret: What does ‘I desire mercy, not sacrifice’ mean, and how does it change the way the Sabbath is kept?
Why does Jesus say that blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven, and how does the context of verses 22 to 28 help explain it?
What is the ‘sign of Jonah’, and why does Jesus refuse any other sign to those who demand one?
